notes.meaning: David ran from Saul to Nob, a town of priests where God's tent of worship then stood. He came for food and also to seek God's guidance in his trouble. Ahimelech the high priest trembled when he saw him. The king's son-in-law had turned up suddenly with no attendants, and the priest feared some danger. What a comfort it is that, in trouble, we have a God to go to.

David told the priest a plain lie. Saul had sent him on no secret mission. Fear made him say it, and his faith grew weak for a moment. Scripture does not hide this sin, and we should not excuse it. The lie later led to the killing of the priests at Nob, and David admitted his guilt. Even God's saints have failings, so no one is good in himself. All of us need God's mercy.

David asked for five loaves, or whatever food was there. He had spoken of young men waiting for him, and he likely wanted enough for two or three days. In those days travelers had to carry their own food, so David had to ask for bread.

The priest had no ordinary bread close at hand, only the holy bread that had been set out before God. Normally only priests could eat it. He was willing to give it in this time of need, but only if the men were ritually clean. That meant they had not slept with their wives in the last few days. Some commentators think the priest first asked God's permission (see 22:10).

David said the men had kept away from women, as they always did on a mission. Their gear, and even their bodies, were clean in God's sight. The bread had already been taken off the Lord's table, so in their need it could be used almost like ordinary bread. Food rules had to give way to the greater law of mercy and need.

So the priest gave David the holy bread, called the Bread of the Presence. It had sat before the Lord for a week before being replaced with fresh loaves. Jesus later used this story when the Pharisees blamed his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath. He showed that God wants mercy more than ritual, and that in real need such rules give way.

An important detail is slipped in here. Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, was at the tabernacle that day. He may have been keeping a vow, or he could not travel because it was the Sabbath. He later betrayed David and the priests to Saul. We cannot always tell what is in the hearts of people who come to God's house.
David then asked for a weapon. He said the king's business was so urgent that he had left without his sword. This was part of the same false story. The priests themselves kept no swords.

The only sword there was Goliath's. It had been kept wrapped up behind the ephod, the high priest's special garment, as a reminder of God's goodness. David said there was none like it. It was large and strong, and it was also a sign of God's favor. Each time he looked at it, it would remind him of what God had already done for him.

David fled out of Saul's land to Achish, the Philistine king of Gath. It was a risky choice, since Gath was Goliath's own city and David carried Goliath's sword. He may have hoped the king would shelter an enemy of Saul. God had promised David the crown, yet here he was an exile. Sometimes God's plans seem to run against his promises, and this tests our faith.

Achish's servants knew David at once. They remembered the song about him killing tens of thousands, many of them Philistines. They called him "king of the land." They may have meant he was Israel's great hero, or that he was Israel's future king. Either way, they saw him as a danger and did not want him kept alive among them.

David took their words to heart and grew very afraid that Achish would kill him. Here he learned what he later taught in the Psalms: it is better to trust the Lord than to trust princes. Matthew Henry links Psalm 56 to this time: "When I am afraid, I will trust in you."

To save his life, David pretended to be insane. He scribbled on the gate doors and let spit run down his beard, which was a deep shame in that culture. The commentators say this pretending cannot be called right. Some say it can be partly excused as a trick of war to escape enemies. Others say plainly that deceit never pleases God.

The trick worked. Achish refused to have a madman in his house and sent David away. Some commentators think Achish saw through the act but went along with it to protect David. Psalm 34 is linked to this escape. It shows that David's heart still trusted the Lord even when things were at their worst.
